transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Corva Coleman.
President Trump says he and his political action committee
will personally pay for the controversial TV ads that have praised him.
Up till now, the ads have said they're paid for by the federal government,
that is American taxpayers.
Critics say these ads are partisan and use Republican talking points.
The president is back at the White House after he signed an executive order
aimed at lowering diesel fuel costs.
Trump signed the order during a campaign rally in Nebraska last night,
as NPR's Franco Ordonez reports.
President Trump told the audience in the middle of agriculture country
that he was signing the order to help farmers.
The rising cost of fuel has been a significant challenge
for Republicans heading into the midterms.
Prices for diesel used by trucks have been hit particularly hard
due to the wars in both Iran and Ukraine.
The president did not share details,
but the order is expected to expand access to diesel,
including so-called red dye diesel fuel,
which is used by the agriculture industry,
and not subject to the same state and federal highway taxes as regular diesel.
Franco Ordonez, NPR News.
The Paramount Skydance and Warner Brothers discovery deal closes today.
And Pierre's Mandalit Del Barco says the merger brings together media giants.
David Ellison will control this new media empire
with help from his billionaire father Larry Ellison
and investors from the Middle East.
Their company Skydance combines two legendary film studios,
both more than 100 years old, Paramount Pictures and Warner Brothers Pictures.
Ellison also gets their streaming services like Paramount Plus and HBO Max.
He gets MTV, Comedy Central, The Food Network,
and two huge news outlets, CNN and CBS News.
And Pierre's Mandalit Del Barco reporting.
Massive student protest marches will be held in Paris
and other French cities today.
The protest movement for better conditions in high schools
is now in its second week.
And Pierre's Eleanor Beardsley reports
it has not lost momentum even though it has been plagued by violence.
French TV news footage is showing students gathering in cities across the country
ahead of protest marches this afternoon.
Even students at well-off high schools in big cities like Paris are taking part.
They say out of solidarity with students in the poorer suburbs
and rural areas where schools are more rundown.
The education minister says some of the students' demands are valid.
The far right has called the students hoodlums that burn their schools
and says the problem is a lack of authority.
The far left says police violence is to blame.
The public is shocked over a 15-year-old boy losing his hand
after a police tear gas stun grenade blew up.
Left-wing unions have called on their members
to accompany the students in their marches today
to make sure there's no violence.
Eleanor Beardsley in Pierre News, Paris.
You're listening to NPR.
Some AI experts testified before the New York City Council yesterday.
They're worried about the dangers of the growing technology.
The New York City Council is reviewing AI development,
but AI company representatives testified and pushed back,
saying they are fully focused on safety.
The U.S. Supreme Court is considering whether a case seeking damages
over the costs of climate change should be allowed to proceed,
and Pierre Kerry Johnson reports on the first oral arguments
of the new term at the high court.
Boulder, Colorado sued Suncor and ExxonMobil to recover money
for the costs of responding to global warming.
That was back in 2018,
but the case has still not reached a jury.
County officials argued the companies knew
but chose to deceive the public about the threats from climate change.
The energy giants are asking the Supreme Court to block the lawsuit
because they say the federal government
should be in charge of such a sweeping issue.
The justices asked tough questions of both sides.
They seem to be weighing a potential flood of cases in state courts
against blocking cases by Boulder and other local governments
at such an early stage.
Kerry Johnson, NPR News.
Disgraced televangelist Jim Baker has died at the age of 86.
That is according to his wife, Lori Baker.
Baker and his former wife, Tammy Faye Baker,
built a Christian TV empire called the PTL Club.
He lost that over a sex scandal and financial crimes
for which Baker spent time in prison.
This is NPR.
Before Bernie Sanders, or AOC,
a man named Michael Harrington tried to market socialism to the American public.
Tens of millions of Americans were poor, miserable, in body and in spirit.
On NPR's Throughline, how the founder of the DSA
created a modern political movement.
Listen to Throughline in the NPR app or wherever you get your podcasts.

topics.text: Trump and his PAC will personally pay for controversial TV ads praising him
Trump signs executive order at Nebraska rally aimed at lowering diesel fuel costs
Paramount Skydance and Warner Brothers discovery merger closes, creating major media conglomerate
Massive student protest marches planned in Paris and French cities over school conditions
AI experts testify before New York City Council about dangers of growing technology
Supreme Court considers whether Boulder Colorado climate change lawsuit against oil companies proceeds
Disgraced televangelist Jim Baker dies at age 86, founded PTL Club with wife
